new_statements.quote: The favorite position for stress is on the third mora from the end of the word (§1:22). Accordingly, a two morae penult is stressed (§6:2); but the antepenult would be stressed when the penult and the ultima each have the value of one mora (§6:4). A less favored position for stress is on the second mora from the end of the word. Accordingly, a two morae ultima is stressed; but the penult would be stressed before a one mora ultima (§6:3). A small class of words shows stress arbitrarily on the theme-final vowel, even when this vowel is the word-end mora (§6:5).

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Unami (qs-tier-2026-09-12) has an empty rule string; our check record codes it as weight-sensitive / right-edge / CVV+CVC heavy on second-hand carriers of Goddard 1979 ('rightmost non-final strong vowel'; LTD 'stress on the next to last vowel'). Formulation differs from Godd…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is counted in morae from the right edge. The usual position is the third mora from the end: a two-mora (long/heavy) penult is stressed, and if both penult and ultima are one mora each the antepenult is stressed. A less common position is the second mora from the end: a two-mora ultima is stressed (final stress), otherwise the penult before a one-mora ultima. Further snippets: some words 'show stress on the second, others on the third mora from the end of the word (§1:39)'; a stressed penult shifts its stress to a preceding prefix when a vowel-initial enclitic particle with intrinsic stress is added ('the stress of its penult will shift to the prefix as soon as the stem or word is combined with an enclitic particle which begins in a vowel and has an intrinsic stress'); in §6:2 'The theme-final vowel is stressed without respect to mora count (§1:39)'. Voegelin's term for stress is 'firm stress' (footnote: 'according to which terminology my "firm stress" is merely "stress"').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress was recovered from the snippets; the only stress terms attested for the Delaware chapter are 'firm stress'/'firm-stressed' (Voegelin's word for stress) and 'unstressed'. (The 'loud / medial / weak stress' snippets in the same volume belong to Trager's Taos chapter, §2:221, and were excluded.)
new_statements.exceptions: (1) 'A small class of words shows stress arbitrarily on the theme-final vowel, even when this vowel is the word-end mora (§6:5)'; §6:2 adds 'The theme-final vowel is stressed without respect to mora count'. (2) Words split between stress on the second and on the third mora from the end (§1:39), the second-mora (final-stress) position being 'less favored'. (3) Morphological shift: penult stress moves to a prefix when a vowel-initial, intrinsically stressed enclitic is added.
new_statements.identity_note: Voegelin's Delaware chapter describes the Oklahoma Delaware around Dewey, which he says 'speak Lenape Delaware as opposed to Munsee Delaware', i.e. (Southern/Oklahoma) Unami, the same variety as the catalog's Unami (unam1242). The chapter-attribution of the stress passage rests on its cross-references to §6:2-§6:5, whose §6:2 snippet ('theme-final vowel remains a or e.. short in word-final and before -hti-t') is the Unami theme-vowel alternation and conjunct 3pl ending, and on the passage ending immediately before the chapter's own '2. PHONOLOGY' heading.

readall_conflicts: No contradiction in placement type: Voegelin 1946 (Oklahoma/Lenape Delaware = Unami) and the carriers of Goddard 1979 already in the record both describe a right-edge, weight-sensitive system with a penult default, antepenult retraction when the penult is light, final stress on a heavy ultima, and marked lexical exceptions. The one point of tension is the formulation: Voegelin counts morae from the right ('third mora from the end' favored, 'second mora from the end' less favored), whereas Goddard's rule (via Hayes 1995, Hagstrom, Wikipedia) assigns strength by a left-to-right alternation of light open syllables plus inherent heaviness, so the two can pick different syllables in strings of light syllables (e.g. three light open syllables: antepenult by Voegelin's mora count, penult by Goddard's even-syllable-strong count). Whether Voegelin's morae include closed syllables or a syllable count cannot be checked from snippets. The snippet reconstruction (no page scan) is the main caveat; every quoted phrase was returned independently by at least two scans with identical surrounding words.

tone.quote: A long vowel preceding a plain consonant falls slightly in pitch and perceived loudness. The long consonants are always voiceless and generally half long, ... they are perceived as ambisyllabic, with level pitch on the preceding vowel. ... The main stress in each word (accompanied by raised pitch in isolation) is marked with an acute accent (´): /kawí/ ‘sleep (you sg.)!’ vs. /káwi/ ‘you (sg.) sleep’. In texts 4 through 14 sentence intonation is tentatively indicated by the following conventions: ↗ Pitch rise on final syllable. ... ↑ Raised pitch register.
